title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: The Dust Heap as Destiny

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — a close, passionate, occasionally argumentative journey through one of the strangest and most magnificent novels in the English language.
I'm your host, and today we begin at the very foundation of Charles Dickens's last completed novel: the dust heap.
Not a metaphor — or not only a metaphor — but an actual mountain of Victorian refuse from which an entire world of money, ambition, and moral reckoning grows.
Three remarkable readers join me today, and I want to introduce each of them properly.

Oliver Trevelyan has given voice to more classic novels in audio than perhaps anyone alive — he hears Dickens as a performer first, catching the comic rhythms, the grotesque delight, the timing written for the voice.
Oliver, welcome.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose reading of the novel is always, first and last, a reading of character — of goodness tested, of will strained, of moral imagination at work.
Edmund, delighted to have you.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read Our Mutual Friend as a teenager and has returned to it many times — she reads for the experience, for what stops you in your tracks on the page.
Caroline, so glad you're here.
Now — the dust heap.
Dickens opens his novel with a dead man in the river and a fortune made from rubbish — and the two are connected from the very first pages.
Oliver, Mortimer Lightwood introduces us to the old Dust Contractor — let's hear what Dickens actually gives him to say.
The thing that strikes me every single time I read this opening is the sheer audacity of it.
Mortimer is at a dinner party, telling the story of the dead man as a kind of parlour entertainment — and he describes the father's estate with this wonderful accumulating rhythm.
Listen to how Dickens builds it — the list just keeps coming, gathering weight:
'Coal-dust, vegetable-dust, bone-dust, crockery dust, rough dust and sifted dust,—all manner of Dust.'
That final 'all manner of Dust' — capitalised, you notice — lands like a full stop on the whole history of the man.
His estate, his character, his geological formation — all of it is Dust.
And Dickens uses that marvellous phrase — 'like an old volcano' — which makes the old man sound both ridiculous and faintly terrifying.
What I love about that passage is the way Dickens lets Mortimer perform it — and you feel the dinner guests being mildly bored, mildly amused.
But underneath the comedy there's something genuinely grotesque about a man who lives in a hollow entirely composed of the things other people threw away.
It gives the word 'wealth' a physical smell.
And then later, when Wegg arrives at the Bower for the first time — Dickens gives us that extraordinary, almost dreamlike image.
The pathway is marked, as the moonlight shows, between two lines of broken crockery set in ashes.
'Certain tall dark mounds rose high against the sky, and where the pathway to the Bower was indicated, as the moonlight showed, between two lines of broken crockery set in ashes.'
Broken crockery set in ashes as a garden path.
That's the estate of a very wealthy man — and Dickens never lets you forget what that wealth is actually made of.
I think one must be careful not to flatten the comedy into polemic — which is a temptation with Dickens, and rather spoils the fun.
The old Dust Contractor is, first and foremost, a comic monster — a splendid creation of grotesque greed.
But I grant you that Dickens doesn't leave it there.
Later in the novel, the narrator addresses the governing classes directly — and the tone shifts from satire to something closer to warning.
The passage runs, if I may:

'My lords and gentlemen and honourable boards, when you in the course of your dust-shovelling and cinder-raking have piled up a mountain of pretentious failure, you must off with your honourable coats for the removal of it, and fall to the work with the power of all the queen's horses and all the queen's men, or it will come rushing down and bury us alive.'
Now that is not the voice of a social theorist — that is the voice of a moralist who fears for the whole edifice.
The dust heap is a warning, not merely a symbol.
Edmund is absolutely right that the voice there is moral rather than theoretical — and it's also extraordinarily physical.
'Off with your honourable coats' — Dickens is telling the lords to roll their sleeves up.
And that final image — 'rushing down and bury us alive' — it's an avalanche of rubbish.
Which, when you think about where we started — the old volcano throwing up its mountain range of Dust — is the same image, turned catastrophic.
There's another passage that stays with me — the journey down to the river at the very start of the novel.
Mortimer and Eugene ride through London toward Gaffer Hexam's — and the prose tracks their descent through the city with extraordinary bleakness.
The line that has never left me since I first read it:
'Accumulated scum of humanity seemed to be washed from higher grounds, like so much moral sewage, and to be pausing until its own weight forced it over the bank and sunk it in the river.'
Moral sewage.
Dickens doesn't flinch — these people are, in the narrator's voice, the city's own waste product.
And the river is waiting for them.
That passage is also, I think, the key to understanding what the river means in this novel.
The Thames is not merely picturesque backdrop — it is the terminus toward which poverty and failure are being gravitationally drawn.
Notice also the detail — 'in and out among vessels that seemed to have got ashore, and houses that seemed to have got afloat.'
Everything is in the wrong place.
The natural order has been inverted — and this, for Dickens, is the social condition he is describing.
Dust above, sewage below — and the whole novel moves between those two poles.
We'll be returning to the river — and to what it takes and what it gives back — throughout this episode.
But next, we turn to the society that floats above all this filth — the Veneerings and their circle — and ask what Dickens does with money once it's been laundered into respectability.

segments.title: Bella's Golden Dream: Beauty and Worth

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
Today we are deep in the heart of what makes this novel so endlessly surprising: the education of Bella Wilfer.
Bella arrives in the story as a self-declared mercenary — a young woman who openly announces she intends to marry for money.
And then Dickens does something extraordinary with her.
Sir Edmund Leigh is with us — retired Oxford don, a critic who reads character as moral test, and one of the sharpest readers of Dickens's heroines I know.
Edmund, Bella's arc is yours today.
Oliver Trevelyan joins us as always — actor, audiobook narrator, and the man who has given voice to more Dickens characters than anyone living.
Oliver hears things in this prose that the rest of us miss.
And Caroline Woodcourt is here — book critic, devoted re-reader of this novel, and the person at this table who will tell you honestly which characters Dickens treats unfairly.
Let us begin with the novel's central wager — can a young woman who confesses to greed actually become genuinely good?
The novel opens its thirty-eighth chapter with a question so compressed it takes your breath away.
Dickens gives us precisely three sentences — and in the middle one, he poses what is really the moral axis of the entire book.
The question is this:
Was the Golden Dustman passing through the furnace of proof and coming out dross?
Furnace of proof — that is an alchemical image, of course, but also a moral one.
Gold goes into the furnace to be tested; dross is what remains when the base metal is all that was ever there.
Dickens is asking whether Boffin — and by implication Bella — will survive their own testing.
And the genius is that Dickens never lets you be quite certain which way it will go.
That chapter-opening — 'We shall know full soon' — is Dickens at his most barefaced.
He is teasing the reader like a showman.
But then he shows us Bella's private crisis — and suddenly it's not a tease at all.
She sits down in her own room, she looks at herself in the looking-glass, and she cross-examines herself with devastating honesty.
Let me read it — because you have to hear the rhythm of her self-interrogation to feel how precise it is:

'Why, what need to excuse him? What he said was very sensible, I am sure, and very true, I am sure. It is only what I often say to myself. Don't I like it then? No, I don't like it, and, though he is my liberal benefactor, I disparage him for it. Then pray, what do you mean by this, you inconsistent little Beast?'
That repeated 'I am sure' — she's not sure at all.
She's trying to convince herself, and the sentence structure gives her away before she does.
What I love about that passage is the looking-glass.
Dickens says 'as usual' — it's a ritual for her.
Bella is her own prosecuting counsel.
She knows what she is doing — she just hasn't yet found the will to stop doing it.
And calling herself a Beast — there's self-laceration there, but also something almost fond.
Dickens is genuinely fond of her too, even in her worst moments.
Precisely — and that is what separates Bella from the merely satirised.
She has the moral intelligence to see her own fault clearly.
What she lacks — at this stage — is what Johnson would have called the power of resolution acting upon conviction.
She knows better; she has not yet chosen better.
Now, one might compare her to Lizzie Hexam — a woman who has chosen, and at enormous personal cost.
Lizzie's account of what Eugene Wrayburn means to her — what she stands to lose if she surrenders that connection — is, to my mind, one of the most morally serious passages in the entire novel.
She says of him:

'I should lose a kind of picture of him — or of what he might have been, if I had been a lady, and he had loved me — which is always with me, and which I somehow feel that I could not do a mean or a wrong thing before.'
Virtue, here, is not a rule but an image carried within.
It is, I think, the most quietly radical moral psychology in Dickens.
That passage undoes me every time.
Because Lizzie is describing a love she has never acted upon, never declared — and yet it has made her.
The image of the hands — coarse from rowing the river, then softened by her new work — that's Dickens doing something almost miraculous with physical detail.
Transformation is written on the body.
Which is exactly what we are watching happen to Bella — from the inside out, rather than the outside in.
And it's Lizzie who sees it first — or rather, who lets Bella be seen.
The narrator describes Bella as having a nature that is —
'wayward, playful, affectionate nature, giddy for want of the weight of some sustaining purpose, and capricious because it was always fluttering among little things.'
Giddy for want of the weight of some sustaining purpose.
That is the most precise diagnosis of Bella's problem — and it implies the cure.
The cure being, of course, to actually have something worth caring about.
And what strikes me as a performer is the father's voice when the moment finally comes.
R. Wilfer — the cherub, bless him — delivers the most winding sentence of moral vindication in the English language.
He speaks of 'the certain mercenary young person distantly related to myself' — meaning his own daughter — and you have to hold the comedy and the tenderness simultaneously:

'the certain mercenary young person distantly related to myself, having previously observed and mentioned to myself that prosperity was spoiling Mr Boffin, felt that she must not sell her sense of what was right and what was wrong, and what was true and what was false, and what was just and what was unjust, for any price that could be paid to her by any one alive.'
The repetitions — right and wrong, true and false, just and unjust — are Wilfer at his most grandly absurd and his most genuinely moving.
He is making a little speech; and the speech is entirely true.
And Bella, having survived that test — the spectacle of Mr Boffin's apparent corruption — then asks for a harder one.
She says to John Rokesmith, with disarming directness:
'Try me through some reverse, John — try me through some trial — and tell them after that, what you think of me.'
This is the language of proof — the same word Dickens used in that opening question about the furnace.
Bella is asking to be tested as gold is tested — and she is confident she will not come out dross.
That, to my mind, is the completion of a genuine moral arc — not a sentimental conversion, but a hard-won change of character.
And what moves me is that she's not claiming perfection.
She says she is 'not half, not a quarter, so much worthier' as she hopes to become.
She is asking to be tested precisely because she doesn't yet fully trust herself.
That is the most honest thing a reformed character can say.
Furnace of proof — it's one of those phrases that gathers meaning as the novel progresses.
Bella enters the fire suspicious, divided against herself — and emerges asking to be tested further still.
In our next segment, we'll turn to the world that surrounds her — the river, the dust, and the money that moves through this novel like a tide.

segments.title: The Comic Grotesques: Wegg, Podsnap, and the Pleasure of the Text

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's last completed novel apart, passage by passage, to see what makes it tick.
I'm your host, and today we are deep in the comedy — the grotesques, the frauds, the magnificent absurdities that crowd every chapter.
With me are three guests who bring very different pleasures to this material.
Oliver Trevelyan has voiced more classic novels than anyone alive, and he hears Dickens the way a musician hears a score — every comic rhythm, every pause for effect.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who believes the novel's greatness lies in its moral imagination — and who will keep us honest when the comedy threatens to swallow the people.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has re-read this novel many times and knows exactly which sentences make her stop and start again.
We begin with the great comic set-pieces — the looking-glass passage, Wegg at his stall, the Lammles' extraordinary ventriloquism.
Oliver — the looking-glass above the Veneerings' sideboard is one of the most dazzling openings in all of Dickens. What does it sound like when you read it aloud?
It sounds like a conjuror warming up — short declarative sentences, each one a flick of the wrist.
Dickens has invented a device — the mirror — so he can introduce his entire social world in a single sustained passage without pausing for breath.
And the repetition — 'Reflects Veneering', 'Reflects Mrs Veneering', 'Reflects Podsnap' — that anaphora is pure performance.
It's a roll-call, a parade, and a prosecution all at once.
The description of Veneering himself is the centrepiece, and it has to be read slowly to land properly.
"Reflects Veneering; forty, wavy-haired, dark, tending to corpulence, sly, mysterious, filmy — a kind of sufficiently well-looking veiled-prophet, not prophesying."
'Not prophesying.' Two words. The whole man in two words.
He has all the trappings of a prophet — the veil, the mystery — and absolutely nothing to say.
And then he turns immediately to Mrs Podsnap, and the comic register shifts completely.
The description of Podsnap himself is already wonderful — those 'two little light-coloured wiry wings' of hair looking 'as like his hairbrushes as his hair.'
But then Mrs Podsnap — 'fine woman for Professor Owen, quantity of bone, neck and nostrils like a rocking-horse.'
'Professor Owen' is the reference to Richard Owen, the anatomist — the man who coined the word 'dinosaur.'
Dickens is saying, politely, that this woman belongs in a natural history museum.
What I love is that it never tips into cruelty — it remains entirely delighted with its own ingenuity.
I take the point about delight, but I would distinguish between two kinds of comic portrait in this passage.
Twemlow is given something approaching pathos — 'cheeks drawn in as if he had made a great effort to retire into himself some years ago, and had got so far and had never got any farther.'
That is not merely a physical description.
It is a portrait of a man who once attempted dignity and became permanently stranded in the attempt.
The Veneerings and Podsnaps are targets. Twemlow is a victim. The moral weight differs enormously.
Edmund is absolutely right to separate them, and a performer feels that distinction the moment he opens his mouth.
Podsnap you play with a kind of happy brutality. Twemlow you play with an ache in the back of the throat.
But it's Wegg — Silas Wegg — who gives me the most sustained pleasure as a performer.
Because Wegg is a fraud who cannot admit his own fraudulence, even to himself. That's a very precise comic idea.
After Boffin leaves his stall, Wegg sits alone and computes his new advantage — and Dickens gives us the most marvellous account of his self-deception.
"Mr Wegg would even have picked a handsome quarrel with any one who should have challenged his deep acquaintance with those aforesaid eight volumes of Decline and Fall."
He has never read a word of Gibbon, obviously.
But the self-deception is so complete, so load-bearing to his sense of himself, that he would fight for it.
And Dickens doesn't leave it as a joke at Wegg's expense. He makes it universal.
'Herein he ranged with that very numerous class of impostors, who are quite as determined to keep up appearances to themselves, as to their neighbours.'
'That very numerous class.' The mild savagery of that phrase.
He is saying: most people do this. Wegg is not an anomaly — he is a magnification.
That's what makes the comedy so unsettling when you sit with it.
And Dickens presses even further when he enlists the taxidermic specimens to witness Wegg's moral deterioration.
The passage in Mr Venus's shop where the preserved creatures observe Wegg's scheming is, I confess, one of the strangest things Dickens ever wrote.
The alligator's smile carries the weight of geological time — the cynicism of the deep past.
"The yard or two of smile on the part of the alligator might have been invested with the meaning, 'All about this was quite familiar knowledge down in the depths of the slime, ages ago.'"
Human treachery is so old, so reliably recurring, that even a preserved reptile has seen it all before.
The comedy is still there, but it has a very dark bottom to it.
That 'yard or two of smile' is the most brilliantly calibrated physical description in the chapter. You feel the length of the jaw.
But I want to talk about the Lammles and the opera box, because that is Dickens at his most technically astonishing.
The Lammles are engineering a romance between Fledgeby and Georgiana Podsnap — and they do it by speaking entirely on the young couple's behalf.
The lovers never actually speak to each other. The Lammles conduct the entire courtship as a ventriloquist act.
Dickens captures the result in one sentence of perfect construction.

"Through this device the two young people conversed at great length and committed themselves to a variety of delicate sentiments, without having once opened their lips, save to say yes or no, and even that not to one another."
'Not to one another.' The cruelest, funniest three words in the scene.
A courtship conducted entirely by proxy. It is the most efficient satire of performance in social life that I know.
Poor Georgiana. She is being sold, essentially, and she has not the faintest idea.
The comedy of the mechanism is real — the Lammles' relay of attributed remarks is genuinely funny to read.
But underneath it is something rather awful — two people being traded in a transaction dressed up as romance.
That's Dickens's particular genius in this novel — he won't let the comedy excuse you from noticing what the comedy is about.
Miss Woodcourt identifies the crucial point. The grotesque and the pathetic are not in competition in this novel — they are the same instrument played in two registers.
Dickens learned from Hogarth — that you may make a man ridiculous and pitiable in the same stroke of the pen.
The looking-glass passage makes us laugh at these people. But we are also, quietly, being indicted alongside them.
We are the guests who came to dinner. We are reflected in the glass too.
That's a remarkable place to land — the reader implicated in the very society being satirised.
Oliver, Edmund, Caroline — that was a magnificent passage through the comic heart of this novel.
In our next segment, we'll move from the pleasure of the comedy to the novel's darker currents — the river, the dust heaps, and what Dickens is doing with death and money.

segments.title: Reading Harmon's Return: Plot, Disguise, and Moral Consequence

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's last completed novel seriously — as the strange, brilliant, morally urgent work it is.
I'm your host, and today we're deep into one of the novel's most extraordinary sequences — the chapters in which John Harmon reveals himself, to us if not yet to the world.
With me are three readers who know this novel inside out.
Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more classic novels than perhaps any living voice actor, and he hears Dickens the way a conductor hears a score — rhythm first, meaning second.

Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose readings of Dickens are grounded in moral character and the tradition of the English novel — and who has no patience for readings that flatten fiction into sociology.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a critic and devoted re-reader who comes to these chapters asking the simplest and most demanding question: what is it actually like to read this?
We're looking at the chapters where Harmon's disguise is laid bare, where we learn why he chose to stay dead, and what that choice costs him.
Oliver, let's begin with the moment of unmasking itself — because Dickens stages it in a way that's almost theatrical.
It is theatrical — and it's also deeply, characteristically Dickensian in the way it refuses to make the revelation a simple triumph.
We have the oakum-headed, oakum-whiskered disguise stripped away in an alleyway — in a moment, the text says, as the favouring wind swept the street clear.
And then comes this extraordinary sentence — let me read it because it needs to be heard.
"became as like that same lost wanted Mr Julius Handford, as never man was like another in this world."
Three identities — Harmon, Rokesmith, Handford — and Dickens collapses them all into one formulation, repeated twice in the same paragraph.
That repetition is everything. It's not a device — it's the whole argument about identity in one sentence.
What strikes me every time I read that passage is how utterly matter-of-fact Dickens is about something that should feel miraculous.
There's no drumroll, no gothic shudder — just the wind, and a coat, and a breast pocket, and the hair and whisker stowed away in a moment.
And that very ordinariness makes the philosophical point for him.
Identity, in this novel, is always partly costume. It's always partly performance.
And the ease with which Harmon shifts between his three selves — in a public alleyway, as the wind passes — is quietly terrifying.
I don't dispute the observation about identity — but I think we must be careful not to make Harmon too protean, too free-floating, as if selfhood were merely theatrical.
What Dickens gives us, I think, is a man who is fractured precisely because he has never been permitted to be himself.
Consider the passage of self-interrogation — it's one of the most revealing moments in the whole novel.
"I came back, shrinking from my father's money, shrinking from my father's memory, mistrustful of being forced on a mercenary wife."
The repetition of 'shrinking' is not mere rhetoric — it is the grammar of a damaged soul.
This is a man formed — or rather deformed — by inheritance in its most literal sense.
Edmund puts his finger on something crucial there — and it leads directly to the gothic quality of the night Harmon nearly died.
Because this is not simply a man recounting a near-drowning — this is a man re-entering a nightmare he can barely hold together in memory.
The setting Dickens gives him is almost absurdly atmospheric — and yet it earns every drop of atmosphere.
"The room overlooked the river, or a dock, or a creek, and the tide was out."
That 'or' construction — river, or dock, or creek — is a masterpiece of uncertainty.
He doesn't know where he was. He can't quite fix reality. And the tidal mud below reflects that perfectly.
That tidal mud — it runs all the way through the novel, doesn't it.
And here it's not background — it's the condition of Harmon's consciousness at that moment.
What I keep returning to is the moment in the public-house, when the decision is made — when staying dead becomes a choice rather than an accident.
Dickens frames it so starkly — and I always stop at this passage.
"the thought entered my head of turning the danger I had passed through, to the account of being for some time supposed to have disappeared mysteriously, and of proving Bella."
'Proving Bella.' Two words. The whole engine of the plot folded into two words.
And yet I'm never quite sure whether to admire him for it or find it troubling.
Caroline's hesitation is, I think, the correct response — and it is, to Dickens's enormous credit, a hesitation he builds into the novel itself.
The chapter that follows is almost a legal brief — Harmon arraigning himself, examining each step that compounded the original deception.
And the diagnosis Dickens offers is as precise as any he ever wrote.

"When in the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil — never yet for good within his knowledge then — of his father and his father's wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of his first deception, it was meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few hours or days."
There is the whole mechanism of moral erosion laid out in one sentence.
A deception intended to be brief, intended to be kind — and then snared into permanence by circumstances that outran his intention.
That is not a villain's story. That is a story about the weakness of good men.
And it culminates in that extraordinary image of the ghost — which is where Dickens, I think, finds the moral resolution that pure argument cannot reach.
After Harmon has spent the night, as Dickens puts it, in the sexton-task of piling earth above John Harmon, he wakes resolved.
And then comes this — and I'd ask you to really hear it.

"No ghost should trouble Mr and Mrs Boffin's peace; invisible and voiceless, the ghost should look on for a little while longer at the state of existence out of which it had departed, and then should for ever cease to haunt the scenes in which it had no place."
'Invisible and voiceless.' He has decided to be a ghost by an act of will.
There's something almost saintly about it — and something quite mad.
Saintly and mad — yes, exactly. That is precisely the tonal tightrope Dickens is walking.
Because if you read that passage coolly, it sounds like self-deception — a man rationalising what suits him.
But Dickens writes it with such tenderness — 'broken morning rest,' 'strengthened in his purpose' — that you feel the genuine moral effort involved.
He is not deceiving others to profit himself. He is choosing to be nobody so that others may flourish.
Whether that justifies the deception is a question the novel leaves beautifully, uncomfortably open.
The ghost who wills himself invisible — and what that costs him when the world insists on seeing him again.
We've been circling the question of whether Harmon's choice is heroic or deluded — and I suspect we'll be circling it for the rest of the episode.
In our next segment, we'll look at what this disguise does to those around him — particularly Bella, and the Boffins — and whether the novel finally vindicates or merely forgives John Harmon.

segments.title: The Music of Dickens's Voice: Rhythms in Crisis and Comedy

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've been tracing character and society through Dickens's great late novel — but this segment turns to the prose itself.
The music of the sentences: the comic timing, the moral weight, the moments where rhythm and meaning become inseparable.
Caroline Woodcourt is our guide here — a critic who reads aloud to think, and whose ear for the verbal texture of fiction is, I'd say, unmatched.
Oliver Trevelyan needs no introduction to any listener who has ever heard a Dickens audiobook — he's performed more of them than I care to count.
And Sir Edmund Leigh is here to remind us, with characteristic precision, that style is never separable from moral vision.
Caroline — you've chosen to begin with the fog.
Yes — because the fog passage near the opening of Book Three is one of those moments where you simply have to stop and read it again.
Dickens does something very particular here: he animates the city as if it were a divided, suffering creature.
Listen to the grammar of this sentence — the way the syntax itself splits in two:
That final phrase — 'wholly neither' — lands like a full stop on the city's entire condition.
Animate and inanimate are set in parallel — blinking, wheezing, choking on one side; the sooty spectre on the other.
And then there's that extraordinary colour gradient — dark yellow, brown, browner, browner, until rusty-black at the heart of the City.
It's a visual tracking shot two centuries before cinema.
And that last line — 'a gigantic catarrh' — I defy anyone to read that aloud without a kind of horrified delight.
The whole passage has been building in weight and darkness — and then he closes with a medical term for a runny nose applied to an entire metropolis.
It's grotesque and precise and genuinely funny — simultaneously.
When I perform this sort of passage, I think of it as a piece of music where the tempo has been building and the composer suddenly drops into a low comic note.
That bathetic landing — it's not accidental.
Dickens has perfect pitch for where to put it.
I'd want to add that the passage does more than paint atmosphere — it enacts a moral predicament.
To be 'divided in purpose between being visible and invisible, and so being wholly neither' — that is precisely the condition of every character who conceals their true identity in this novel.
The fog is the social atmosphere in which self-fashioning — and deception — become not merely possible but necessary.
One thinks of John Harmon, of Boffin's elaborate performance, of Headstone beneath his schoolmaster's respectability.
This is style as diagnosis — not decoration.
And when Dickens turns that same diagnostic precision onto human nature rather than the weather, the effect can be devastating.
There's a short passage in the Riderhood scene — the resuscitation — that I find almost unbearable in its compression.
Riderhood has nearly drowned, and a small crowd has gathered around him with something like compassion — the conditional mercy that proximity to death briefly unlocks.
And then Dickens says, in eight words that I think constitute one of the cruelest sentences in the English novel:
The chiasmus is exact — and merciless.
He warms; they cool. His face softens; their hearts harden.
It's a moral equation in the form of a rhetorical figure — and it says something about human sympathy that no amount of discursive prose could manage.
That passage is almost impossible to read aloud without slowing to a halt.
Because the rhythm insists on it — 'As he grows warm, the doctor and the four men cool' — there's a kind of terrible balance, like scales tipping.
And then: 'As his lineaments soften with life, their faces and their hearts harden to him.'
The word 'lineaments' — that formal, almost anatomical word for the features of a face — it distances us just enough to make the judgment clinical.
Dickens doesn't need to editorialize.
The sentence structure does the condemning.
It is, as Mr. Trevelyan says, economical to a degree that approaches the lapidary.
And yet I'd note that Dickens does not quite damn the bystanders absolutely.
They were moved — briefly, genuinely — by Riderhood's extremity.
The narrator calls it, with beautiful exactness, 'the short-lived delusion.'
Not a lie, not a pretence — a delusion: something they genuinely, if momentarily, believed.
The precision of that word choice is itself a kind of mercy — directed, perhaps, at the reader who feels something similar.
Let's turn from the tragic to the comic — and from Riderhood to someone rather more sympathetic.
Caroline, you've also been looking at two passages involving Bella — one with her father, one revealing something about the prose beneath the playfulness.
The Bella passages reward close attention precisely because Dickens hides his most serious work inside apparently light domestic scenes.
Here she is with her father — feeding him, teasing him, treating him like a plaything, which she always has done.
And then the narrator introduces a note — almost parenthetical — that changes everything.
He writes — and the perspective here belongs to John Rokesmith, watching his wife:
'Underlying seriousness' — that phrase lodges in the mind like a splinter.
Bella knows something she hasn't told her husband yet.
And Dickens encodes that knowledge in a tonal shift so slight you might almost miss it — if you weren't reading carefully.
You'd catch it if you were performing it, though — you'd feel the floor shift under you.
Because the voice that's been light and playful — 'hold his fork by the handle, like a polite child' — suddenly carries ballast.
That contrast — the comedy of the scene and the weight Dickens threads through it — is one of the things that makes the later chapters of this novel so satisfying.
And then there's Mrs. Boffin on her husband — which is in an entirely different register, and absolutely irresistible.
She describes how Boffin would come home at night, having spent the day playing the miser, and — I have to read this:
A man hugging himself for the pleasure of having pretended to be cruel.
It's comic, it's tender, and it's also — underneath — a portrait of the actor's own peculiar joy.
The passage is delightful, certainly.
But I think it does more than entertain.
Mrs. Boffin's account — 'Better and better, old lady. What did we say of her? She'll come through it, the true golden gold' — is a vindication of the moral imagination.
Boffin endured being thought a villain so that Bella might discover her own worth.
That is not merely a comic ruse — it is a species of self-sacrifice, conducted with something very close to love.
The comedy is the medium; the moral is the message.
And notice how Mrs. Boffin's voice carries the comedy — that breathless reported speech — while Dickens slips in the pathos beneath it.
'Laugh, he would, till John and me was often forced to slap his back, and bring it out of his windpipes with a little water.'
It's farce — unashamedly — but the laughter it describes is the laughter of goodness, of people who have done a quietly heroic thing.
That's what Dickens does at his best — he makes you laugh and then you notice, with mild surprise, that you've also been moved.
The comedy and the gravity — inseparable in the end, as this novel always insists.
Thank you, Caroline, Oliver, Edmund — that was a pleasure and a lesson in how to read.
In our next segment, we turn to the river — the great dark artery that runs through Our Mutual Friend and never quite lets you forget it's there.

segments.title: Money, Dust, and Social Machinery: What Boffin Inherits

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We're diving today into one of the novel's most unsettling and brilliantly sustained ironies: what inherited wealth actually does to a good man.
Noddy Boffin — the Golden Dustman — begins the novel as perhaps the most genuinely warm-hearted figure in all of Dickens.
And then the gold dust settles on him, and something darkens.
To help us unpack this, I'm joined as ever by Oliver Trevelyan, who has read more Dickens aloud than almost any living person — and brings the performer's ear to every page.
By Sir Edmund Leigh, whose conviction that great fiction is ultimately about moral character rather than social machinery will, I suspect, be tested today.
And by Caroline Woodcourt, who comes to this novel as a close and deeply devoted reader, attuned to every shift in Dickens's verbal music.
Oliver — let's begin with the moment Boffin and Mrs Boffin arrive at their mansion and London descends upon them.
What does Dickens do there, in purely technical terms?
What he does is give you a sentence that demands to be performed — it almost performs itself, if you're not careful.
The writing is entomological, almost — crawling, creeping, fluttering, buzzing.
He's describing London's aspirant classes as an infestation.
And the sentence opens with this irresistible biblical fanfare — 'behold' — as though we're being invited to witness a spectacle of the age.
Listen to what he actually writes:
"behold all manner of crawling, creeping, fluttering, and buzzing creatures, attracted by the gold dust of the Golden Dustman!"
Four verbs of motion, each one more undignified than the last.
Dickens is having enormous fun — but the contempt underneath the fun is absolute.
I wouldn't quarrel with the brilliance of the image — one never quarrels with Dickens's images, one simply submits.
But I think Oliver's word, 'infestation,' is actually worth examining rather carefully.
Because the creatures are not the wealthy — they are those attracted to wealth.
The satire is aimed at the sycophants and climbers, the people who have made the gold dust their god.
What interests me more, though, is the moral ground from which the Boffins themselves begin.
When Dickens shows us Noddy Boffin confronting his obligations to the fortune, there's a beautiful moment of moral reluctance — not calculation, but genuine unease.
His wife has made the argument for duty, and he replies — with perfect simplicity:
"I suppose we must."
Three words — and Dickens has given us a man who is good in the way that quiet, undemonstrative people are good.
That is the character the novel then puts under siege.
That line stopped me the first time I read it, and it still stops me.
The weight of the whole novel is in that resigned, decent 'I suppose we must.'
Dickens notes that Boffin has a deep respect for his wife's intuitive wisdom — and that respect is itself a form of goodness.
Which is why the passage about his mornings is so unbearably sad to read, once you've seen where the story goes.
Dickens describes how Boffin always begins each day in something like his old self.
"It was as the day went on that the clouds gathered, and the brightness of the morning became obscured."
The image is almost classical — a pastoral morning that darkens into corruption.
And it makes you feel the loss of him, because there's still something to lose.
What I find extraordinary about that passage is its technical precision.
Dickens is doing something very specific — he's making Boffin's corruption follow the rhythm of the sun.
The shadows of avarice lengthen as his own shadow lengthens.
It's a clock — and it's a moral clock.
And then comes the morning that breaks the pattern entirely.
Dickens sets it up with real menace:
"it was black midnight with the Golden Dustman when he first appeared."
Not clouded morning — black midnight, at breakfast.
The solar metaphor collapses, and we're in something much darker.
Oliver is quite right, and I want to press on that detail about the clenched fist.
Dickens writes that Boffin directs a look at Rokesmith's retreating figure that is 'so cunningly malignant.'
And then he secretly threatens him — 'secretly' is the operative word — with a clenched fist once the door is closed.
What we're watching is not simply greed — it's the cowardice that greed produces.
The man who once said 'I suppose we must' with simple, decent resignation now raises a hidden fist.
That is Dickens's moral argument, and it is a serious one — regardless of the comic register he sustains.
What's remarkable is that Bella sees it.
Dickens says she 'would have sat astounded and indignant' — and then he slides past it, almost casually.
The witnessing is important — Bella's education in what wealth does to people is happening in real time.
And this is the morning after Mrs Lammle's intervention — so the corruption has an external catalyst.
The novel refuses to let wealth operate in isolation — it needs confederates, flatterers, those crawling and creeping creatures Oliver read to us.
They feed it.
And that ecosystem — the gold dust and its attendant creatures — is really the social machinery the novel is examining throughout.
We've seen Boffin arrive in his mansion bright with possibility, watched the clouds gather across his mornings, and witnessed the darkness arrive full and absolute.
In our next segment, we'll follow the money further — to what it means for those who have never had it, and those who believe they deserve it.

segments.title: Closing: The Novel's Redemption—Love Against the Dust

utterances.text: We've arrived at the closing chapter of our conversation — and, fittingly, at the closing movement of the novel itself.
Our Mutual Friend ends not with the dust-heaps, not with the Thames, but with something Dickens insists on pressing into our hands: redemption.
Bella is transformed. John Harmon is resurrected. Wrongs are set right, chains of debt and obligation carefully unwound.
And Dickens himself steps forward — almost defiantly — to tell us he knew exactly what he was doing all along.
Oliver, Edmund, Caroline — does the ending earn it?
I want to begin with Bella, because Bella's confession is one of the moments in this novel that absolutely stops me.
She's covering her face with her hands — that stage direction Dickens gives us — and she says something that is almost too vulnerable to be borne.
The line runs like this:

'It is, how John could love me so when I so little deserved it, and how you, Mr and Mrs Boffin, could be so forgetful of yourselves, and take such pains and trouble, to make me a little better, and after all to help him to so unworthy a wife.'
That phrase — 'so unworthy a wife' — is not false modesty. It's the real thing.
Bella has genuinely looked at herself and found herself wanting. And the novel rewards that honesty rather than punishing it.
That is Dickens in his most generous mode — and I find it, frankly, irresistible.
Oliver is right to single out that moment, and I think it illuminates what the novel is finally about at its moral core.
The reformation of Bella Wilfer is not a social programme. It is an education of the will — the hardest kind of education there is.
She begins the novel mercenary, vain, self-absorbed — and not unknowingly so. She knows her faults and finds them rather entertaining.
By the end, she has passed through something — call it trial, call it grace — that has made her capable of genuine gratitude.
The Boffins' elaborate scheme — and John's long patience — are acts of moral imagination on Dickens's part, not merely plot machinery.
Dr Johnson observed that we are more easily moved by example than by precept. The Boffins teach Bella by showing her what money does to a person — and she learns.
What strikes me is the texture of that moment — 'covering her face with her hands.' Dickens doesn't let her look at them when she says it.
There's something about the shame of being loved beyond what you think you deserve — it's almost unbearable to receive directly.
And then she says, simply: 'But I am very very grateful.' Two 'very's. That doubling is not carelessness — it's Dickens catching the stammer of real feeling.
I've re-read that passage many times and the 'very very' always catches me.
And then Dickens does something I find endlessly charming — he brings in Mr Inspector.
John and Mrs Harmon set about correcting every wrong that had strayed — and the net they cast is wonderfully wide.
Riah, the dolls' dressmaker — even the Inspector himself, 'trepanned into an industrious hunt on a false scent.'
The rumour that reaches us about Inspector is delivered with such comic precision:
that he 'didn't stand to lose a farthing' through Mr Harmon's coming to life, but was quite as well satisfied as if that gentleman had been barbarously murdered.
'Barbarously murdered.' The equanimity of the man is magnificent.
It's Dickens reminding us, even at the close, that comedy and tenderness are not opposites — they're the same breath.
That passage about John and Mrs Harmon setting wrongs right deserves a moment's pause, because it embodies a very particular vision of moral responsibility.
They apply what the text calls 'a very broad and free construction' — including people whose connection to John's fictitious death is indirect at best.
This is not legal duty. This is something closer to what Burke might call the obligations of the affections — duties felt rather than owed.
It gives the lie to any reading of Dickens as merely a sentimentalist. This is a rigorous moral imagination at work.
And then there's the moment where Dickens himself appears — steps out of the fiction entirely, looks us in the eye, and says: I knew.
He's addressing — with barely concealed exasperation — readers who thought the Harmon mystery was bungled.
And he writes this extraordinary sentence:

'I foresaw the likelihood that a class of readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he.'
The symmetry of that — 'at great pains to conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest' — is itself a demonstration of the artistry he's defending.
He's not just arguing for himself. He's arguing for patience with art — for the idea that an artist may be trusted to know what he is about.
Reading that, I always feel a little chastened — and then deeply persuaded.
What I love about that authorial intervention is the nerve of it.
He doesn't apologise. He doesn't explain the solution as though solving a puzzle. He says: concede me a little patience, and trust me.
And if you've read the whole novel — if you've come through the dust-heaps and the river and Rogue Riderhood and Betty Higden — you have conceded him that patience.
And he has — by any measure I know — earned it.
There is a word in that passage that I keep returning to: 'ingenuity.'
He says, 'pleasing myself with the idea that the supposition might in part arise out of some ingenuity in the story.'
Note the delicacy of 'in part' and 'some.' He is not boasting. He is — with magnificent self-possession — allowing that he might have been rather clever.
That is the voice of an artist who trusts his work enough not to oversell it.
Bella's gratitude. The Harmons' wide net of restitution. And Dickens, looking over his shoulder at us, refusing to be anything less than confident in his art.
It's a remarkable closing movement — comic, tender, and oddly defiant all at once.
Oliver, Edmund, Caroline — it has been a genuine pleasure to think through this novel with you.
Our Mutual Friend is a novel that repays every hour given to it — and then asks for more.
To our listeners: thank you for spending this time with us and with Dickens.
We'll be back with another novel — but for now, the dust settles, the river runs, and we leave John and Bella to their happiness.

Left alone at his stall as the other ambled off, Mr Wegg subsided into his
      screen, produced a small pocket-handkerchief of a penitentially-scrubbing
      character, and took himself by the nose with a thoughtful aspect. Also,
      while he still grasped that feature, he directed several thoughtful looks
      down the street, after the retiring figure of Mr Boffin. But, profound
      gravity sat enthroned on Wegg’s countenance. For, while he considered
      within himself that this was an old fellow of rare simplicity, that this
      was an opportunity to be improved, and that here might be money to be got
      beyond present calculation, still he compromised himself by no admission
      that his new engagement was at all out of his way, or involved the least
      element of the ridiculous. Mr Wegg would even have picked a handsome
      quarrel with any one who should have challenged his deep acquaintance with
      those aforesaid eight volumes of Decline and Fall. His gravity was
      unusual, portentous, and immeasurable, not because he admitted any doubt
      of himself but because he perceived it necessary to forestall any doubt of

      impostors, who are quite as determined to keep up appearances to
      themselves, as to their neighbours.

c21:p117.best_quote: Through this device the two young people conversed at great length and committed themselves to a variety of delicate sentiments, without having once opened their lips, save to say yes or no, and even that not to one another.

c30:p3.text:
Here he ceased to be the oakum-headed, oakum-whiskered man on whom Miss
      Pleasant Riderhood had looked, and, allowing for his being still wrapped
      in a nautical overcoat, became as like that same lost wanted Mr Julius
      Handford, as never man was like another in this world. In the breast of
      the coat he stowed the bristling hair and whisker, in a moment, as the
      favouring wind went with him down a solitary place that it had swept clear
      of passengers. Yet in that same moment he was the Secretary also, Mr
      Boffin’s Secretary. For John Rokesmith, too, was as like that same lost
      wanted Mr Julius Handford as never man was like another in this world.
c30:p3.summary: The oakum-headed disguised man removes his false hair and whisker, revealing himself to be John Harmon, who is also the Secretary John Rokesmith, all three identities being the same lost and wanted Julius Handford.
c30:p3.best_quote: became as like that same lost wanted Mr Julius Handford, as never man was like another in this world

c30:p7.text:
‘When I came to England, attracted to the country with which I had none
      but most miserable associations, by the accounts of my fine inheritance
      that found me abroad, I came back, shrinking from my father’s money,
      shrinking from my father’s memory, mistrustful of being forced on a
      mercenary wife, mistrustful of my father’s intention in thrusting that
      marriage on me, mistrustful that I was already growing avaricious,
      mistrustful that I was slackening in gratitude to the two dear noble
      honest friends who had made the only sunlight in my childish life or that
      of my heartbroken sister. I came back, timid, divided in my mind, afraid
      of myself and everybody here, knowing of nothing but wretchedness that my
      father’s wealth had ever brought about. Now, stop, and so far think it
      out, John Harmon. Is that so? That is exactly so.
c30:p7.summary: John Harmon explains that he returned to England reluctantly, conflicted about his inherited wealth, fearful of a mercenary marriage, and anxious about his own character.
c30:p7.best_quote: I came back, shrinking from my father's money, shrinking from my father's memory, mistrustful of being forced on a mercenary wife

c30:p14.text:
‘It is my conviction that we cannot have gone a mile from that shop,
      before we came to the wall, the dark doorway, the flight of stairs, and
      the room. The night was particularly dark and it rained hard. As I think
      the circumstances back, I hear the rain splashing on the stone pavement of
      the passage, which was not under cover. The room overlooked the river, or
      a dock, or a creek, and the tide was out. Being possessed of the time down
      to that point, I know by the hour that it must have been about low water;
      but while the coffee was getting ready, I drew back the curtain (a
      dark-brown curtain), and, looking out, knew by the kind of reflection
      below, of the few neighbouring lights, that they were reflected in tidal
      mud.
c30:p14.summary: John Harmon recalls the room they entered, noting its proximity to the river, the rainy weather, the low tide, and his observation of the dark curtain and tidal mud below.
c30:p14.best_quote: The room overlooked the river, or a dock, or a creek, and the tide was out.

c30:p22.text:
‘I have checked the calculation often, and it must have been two nights
      that I lay recovering in that public-house. Let me see. Yes. I am sure it
      was while I lay in that bed there, that the thought entered my head of
      turning the danger I had passed through, to the account of being for some
      time supposed to have disappeared mysteriously, and of proving Bella. The
      dread of our being forced on one another, and perpetuating the fate that
      seemed to have fallen on my father’s riches—the fate that they
      should lead to nothing but evil—was strong upon the moral timidity
      that dates from my childhood with my poor sister.
c30:p22.summary: While recovering in the public-house, John Harmon decides to let himself remain dead for a time to prove Bella's character and avoid perpetuating his father's wealth's curse.
c30:p22.best_quote: the thought entered my head of turning the danger I had passed through, to the account of being for some time supposed to have disappeared mysteriously, and of proving Bella

c31:p1.text:
He went over it all again. He had lapsed into the condition in which he
      found himself, as many a man lapses into many a condition, without
      perceiving the accumulative power of its separate circumstances. When in
      the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil—never
      yet for good within his knowledge then—of his father and his
      father’s wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of
      his first deception, it was meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few
      hours or days, it was to involve in it only the girl so capriciously
      forced upon him and upon whom he was so capriciously forced, and it was
      honestly meant well towards her. For, if he had found her unhappy in the
      prospect of that marriage (through her heart inclining to another man or
      for any other cause), he would seriously have said: ‘This is another of
      the old perverted uses of the misery-making money. I will let it go to my
      and my sister’s only protectors and friends.’ When the snare into which he
      fell so outstripped his first intention as that he found himself placarded
      by the police authorities upon the London walls for dead, he confusedly
      accepted the aid that fell upon him, without considering how firmly it
      must seem to fix the Boffins in their accession to the fortune. When he
      saw them, and knew them, and even from his vantage-ground of inspection
      could find no flaw in them, he asked himself, ‘And shall I come to life to
      dispossess such people as these?’ There was no good to set against the
      putting of them to that hard proof. He had heard from Bella’s own lips
      when he stood tapping at the door on that night of his taking the
      lodgings, that the marriage would have been on her part thoroughly
      mercenary. He had since tried her, in his own unknown person and supposed
      station, and she not only rejected his advances but resented them. Was it
      for him to have the shame of buying her, or the meanness of punishing her?
      Yet, by coming to life and accepting the condition of the inheritance, he
      must do the former; and by coming to life and rejecting it, he must do the
      latter.
c31:p1.summary: Rokesmith justifies his original deception as harmless, traces how it spiralled beyond his control, and wrestles with the impossible choice between disgracing Bella or deceiving the Boffins.
c31:p1.best_quote: When in the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil—never yet for good within his knowledge then—of his father and his father's wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of his first deception, it was meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few hours or days.

c31:p0.text:
The sexton-task of piling earth above John Harmon all night long, was not
      conducive to sound sleep; but Rokesmith had some broken morning rest, and
      rose strengthened in his purpose. It was all over now. No ghost should
      trouble Mr and Mrs Boffin’s peace; invisible and voiceless, the ghost
      should look on for a little while longer at the state of existence out of
      which it had departed, and then should for ever cease to haunt the scenes
      in which it had no place.
c31:p0.summary: Rokesmith, having symbolically 'buried' John Harmon overnight, wakes resolved to maintain his disguise and protect the Boffins' peace by remaining dead to the world.
c31:p0.best_quote: No ghost should trouble Mr and Mrs Boffin's peace; invisible and voiceless, the ghost should look on for a little while longer at the state of existence out of which it had departed, and then should for ever cease to haunt the scenes in which it had no place.

c34:p0.text:
It was a foggy day in London, and the fog was heavy and dark. Animate
      London, with smarting eyes and irritated lungs, was blinking, wheezing,
      and choking; inanimate London was a sooty spectre, divided in purpose
      between being visible and invisible, and so being wholly neither.
      Gaslights flared in the shops with a haggard and unblest air, as knowing
      themselves to be night-creatures that had no business abroad under the
      sun; while the sun itself when it was for a few moments dimly indicated
      through circling eddies of fog, showed as if it had gone out and were
      collapsing flat and cold. Even in the surrounding country it was a foggy
      day, but there the fog was grey, whereas in London it was, at about the
      boundary line, dark yellow, and a little within it brown, and then
      browner, and then browner, until at the heart of the City—which call
      Saint Mary Axe—it was rusty-black. From any point of the high ridge
      of land northward, it might have been discerned that the loftiest
      buildings made an occasional struggle to get their heads above the foggy
      sea, and especially that the great dome of Saint Paul’s seemed to die
      hard; but this was not perceivable in the streets at their feet, where the
      whole metropolis was a heap of vapour charged with muffled sound of
      wheels, and enfolding a gigantic catarrh.
c34:p0.summary: A richly detailed description of heavy London fog that obscures the city, making it simultaneously visible and invisible, with vivid imagery of gaslight, collapsed sun, and the metropolis transformed into vaporous chaos.
c34:p0.best_quote: Animate London, with smarting eyes and irritated lungs, was blinking, wheezing, and choking; inanimate London was a sooty spectre, divided in purpose between being visible and invisible, and so being wholly neither.

c36:p28.text:
The short-lived delusion begins to fade. The low, bad, unimpressible face
      is coming up from the depths of the river, or what other depths, to the
      surface again. As he grows warm, the doctor and the four men cool. As his
      lineaments soften with life, their faces and their hearts harden to him.

c36:p28.best_quote: As he grows warm, the doctor and the four men cool. As his lineaments soften with life, their faces and their hearts harden to him

c55:p126.text:
While he took his supper, Bella sat by him, sometimes admonishing him to
      hold his fork by the handle, like a polite child, and at other times
      carving for him, or pouring out his drink. Fantastic as it all was, and
      accustomed as she ever had been to make a plaything of her good father,
      ever delighted that she should put him to that account, still there was an
      occasional something on Bella’s part that was new. It could not be said
      that she was less playful, whimsical, or natural, than she always had
      been; but it seemed, her husband thought, as if there were some rather
      graver reason than he had supposed for what she had so lately said, and as
      if throughout all this, there were glimpses of an underlying seriousness.
c55:p126.summary: The narrator notes that beneath Bella's playfulness, there is an undercurrent of seriousness that suggests a deeper emotional or moral concern.
c55:p126.best_quote: "it seemed, her husband thought, as if there were some rather graver reason than he had supposed for what she had so lately said, and as if throughout all this, there were glimpses of an underlying seriousness."

c63:p40.text:
‘But, bless you,’ pursued Mrs Boffin, ‘if you could have seen him of a
      night, at that time of it! The way he’d sit and chuckle over himself! The
      way he’d say “I’ve been a regular brown bear to-day,” and take himself in
      his arms and hug himself at the thoughts of the brute he had pretended.
      But every night he says to me: “Better and better, old lady. What did we
      say of her? She’ll come through it, the true golden gold. This’ll be the
      happiest piece of work we ever done.” And then he’d say, “I’ll be a
      grislier old growler to-morrow!” and laugh, he would, till John and me was
      often forced to slap his back, and bring it out of his windpipes with a
      little water.’
c63:p40.summary: Mrs Boffin fondly describes how Mr Boffin would laugh at night about his performance as a harsh master, reveling in his pretense, and repeatedly reassure them that Bella would prove worthy.
c63:p40.best_quote: The way he'd say "I've been a regular brown bear to-day," and take himself in his arms and hug himself at the thoughts of the brute he had pretended.

Mr Boffin, who had a deep respect for his wife’s intuitive wisdom,
      replied, though rather pensively: ‘I suppose we must.’

c48:p0.text:
The breakfast table at Mr Boffin’s was usually a very pleasant one, and
      was always presided over by Bella. As though he began each new day in his
      healthy natural character, and some waking hours were necessary to his
      relapse into the corrupting influences of his wealth, the face and the
      demeanour of the Golden Dustman were generally unclouded at that meal. It
      would have been easy to believe then, that there was no change in him. It
      was as the day went on that the clouds gathered, and the brightness of the
      morning became obscured. One might have said that the shadows of avarice
      and distrust lengthened as his own shadow lengthened, and that the night
      closed around him gradually.
c48:p0.summary: Mr Boffin typically begins each day in his natural state before wealth's corrupting influence takes hold over the course of the day, gradually darkening his character like lengthening shadows.
c48:p0.best_quote: It was as the day went on that the clouds gathered, and the brightness of the morning became obscured.

c48:p1.text:
But, one morning long afterwards to be remembered, it was black midnight
      with the Golden Dustman when he first appeared. His altered character had
      never been so grossly marked. His bearing towards his Secretary was so
      charged with insolent distrust and arrogance, that the latter rose and
      left the table before breakfast was half done. The look he directed at the
      Secretary’s retiring figure was so cunningly malignant, that Bella would
      have sat astounded and indignant, even though he had not gone the length
      of secretly threatening Rokesmith with his clenched fist as he closed the
      door. This unlucky morning, of all mornings in the year, was the morning
      next after Mr Boffin’s interview with Mrs Lammle in her little carriage.
c48:p1.summary: On the morning after meeting with Mrs Lammle, Boffin exhibits his worst behavior yet, openly hostile and contemptuous toward his Secretary Rokesmith, even threatening him with a clenched fist.
c48:p1.best_quote: His altered character had never been so grossly marked.

c67:p57.text:
When I devised this story, I foresaw the likelihood that a class of
      readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to
      conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John
      Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he. Pleasing myself
      with the idea that the supposition might in part arise out of some
      ingenuity in the story, and thinking it worth while, in the interests of
      art, to hint to an audience that an artist (of whatever denomination) may
      perhaps be trusted to know what he is about in his vocation, if they will
      concede him a little patience, I was not alarmed by the anticipation.
c67:p57.summary: Dickens explains that he intentionally created ambiguity about John Harmon's identity and asks readers to trust his artistic judgment and patience with the serialized format.
c67:p57.best_quote: I foresaw the likelihood that a class of readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he.

c63:p71.text:
‘O yes!’ cried Bella, covering her face with her hands; ‘but that I never
      shall be able to understand as long as I live. It is, how John could love
      me so when I so little deserved it, and how you, Mr and Mrs Boffin, could
      be so forgetful of yourselves, and take such pains and trouble, to make me
      a little better, and after all to help him to so unworthy a wife. But I am
      very very grateful.’
c63:p71.summary: Bella confesses her inability to comprehend how John could love her despite her unworthiness, and how the Boffins could invest such effort in her improvement and reformation.
c63:p71.best_quote: It is, how John could love me so when I so little deserved it, and how you, Mr and Mrs Boffin, could be so forgetful of yourselves, and take such pains and trouble, to make me a little better, and after all to help him to so unworthy a wife.

Mr and Mrs John Harmon’s first delightful occupation was, to set all
      matters right that had strayed in any way wrong, or that might, could,
      would, or should, have strayed in any way wrong, while their name was in
      abeyance. In tracing out affairs for which John’s fictitious death was to
      be considered in any way responsible, they used a very broad and free
      construction; regarding, for instance, the dolls’ dressmaker as having a
      claim on their protection, because of her association with Mrs Eugene
      Wrayburn, and because of Mrs Eugene’s old association, in her turn, with
      the dark side of the story. It followed that the old man, Riah, as a good
      and serviceable friend to both, was not to be disclaimed. Nor even Mr
      Inspector, as having been trepanned into an industrious hunt on a false
      scent. It may be remarked, in connexion with that worthy officer, that a
      rumour shortly afterwards pervaded the Force, to the effect that he had
      confided to Miss Abbey Potterson, over a jug of mellow flip in the bar of
      the Six Jolly Fellowship Porters, that he ‘didn’t stand to lose a
      farthing’ through Mr Harmon’s coming to life, but was quite as well
      satisfied as if that gentleman had been barbarously murdered, and he (Mr
      Inspector) had pocketed the government reward.
c66:p0.summary: John and Mrs Harmon begin correcting wrongs caused by his supposed death, extending protection and aid to various characters including Riah and the dolls' dressmaker, while Inspector gossips about his satisfaction with Harmon's return.
